states.changed: A visitor meets 'in time' read as a window: for each of the 74 deeds of the house's log that Git holds, a black bar from the deed to the first later commit a revert of it would collide with (a median of 7.5 hours), and the mending as a dot inside it (14 of 71) or after it (57); sets the clock's zero at the deed or at the day the log wrote it down, and watches the lanes move; lays a law's clock of 24 hours, 72 hours or 15 days over every lane; learns that the house's 11,783 commits hold no revert; and reads the seven clocks the law sets for an event, five of them starting at the reporter's awareness, none at the event.

A visitor now also meets the programme's own answers: one lane for each of six corrections its state records, with the work that first wrote the wrong figure or sentence, every work that took it over (eight before the correction, three after), the correction as a red stroke, and how many pages still assert it today; learns that only one correction came while the wording stood in one work, and that the three made in the state reached none of the works that held them: six pages of its siblings still assert them after this practice marked its own six; opens any lane for its pages and readings.

A visitor now meets the check at the top of the work, eight findings marked held, corrected, withdrawn or answered: 'another hand' withdrawn, since 55 of the 61 windows a later commit closed were closed under the deed's own Git name; 32 commits that undo an earlier one exactly without Git's sentence, none of them a deed of the log; the log's day read as a decision log's; the clocks split into five of law and two voluntary; section IV with one case withdrawn, the step-1 rise found on three more pages as '334 times', and the state's corrections shown reaching the Studio's and the Field's pages once they were addressed, beside the state's own note of 15 November that was addressed to no one and still stands; and, in section II, the Field's question answered: the window clocks the first write over a deed, not the first sight of it.

A visitor now meets the window first, section I's lanes and toggles at the top, under one sentence that says what 'another hand' can mean in this house's Git (another commit on a deed's lines, never another person or machine); in section IV walks one correction, the counted stock's rise, station by station along a time line from the work that first wrote it, through every work that took it over, the state's correction and its note of 15 November addressed to no one, to the two offers that addressed it to the Studio and the Studio's marks, and on to today, when no page a visitor meets asserts it; and in section V finds Kiener (2025) answered: 61 of the 75 deeds read at their commits stand under the architect's Git name alone, so the record that makes him answerable cannot say whether he or a session acted, the finding the Field's reading 93 codes as one of the six of 28 that rest on this house's own Git and log.
